data.title: Keysight Technologies perks up on strong Q4 results, guidance
data.description:
Keysight Technologies (KEYS) shares rose 2.7% in extended trading on Thursday as the tech company reported fiscal fourth-quarter results that topped Wall Street's estimates.

For the period ending Oct. 31, Keysight said it earned an adjusted $3.61 per share as revenue rose 41% year-over-year to come in at $1.99B. Analysts had expected the company to earn an adjusted $3.37 per share on $1.95B in revenue.

“Keysight delivered the strongest year in the company’s history, with robust order and revenue growth and significant earnings per share expansion,” said Satish Dhanasekaran, Keysight’s President and CEO, in a statement. “As we look ahead, the investments we have made to differentiate our portfolio position us to deliver growth and outperform our markets in fiscal 2027.”

Looking to the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Keysight expects to earn between $3.63 and $3.69 per share on an adjusted basis, above the $3.21 analysts forecast. Sales are forecast to be between $2.04B and $2.06B, above the $1.96B that analysts expected.

The company will host a conference call at 4:30 p.m. EST to discuss the results.

data.title: Valvoline climbs 10% on fiscal 2027 outlook, Q4 results
data.description:
Automotive maintenance company Valvoline (VVV) rose just over 10% on Thursday following its fiscal fourth-quarter results and fiscal 2027 outlook. The stock ended the day at $36.79, rising $3.42 on the day.

The company reported revenue of approximately $554 million, which missed the cited estimate, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.42, which was in line. Management projected fiscal 2027 same-store sales growth of 5% to 7% and adjusted EPS of $1.85 to $2.05.

data.title: Intuit meets FQ1 earnings estimates, Credit Karma hits guidance, Mailchimp sale disclosed
data.description:
Intuit's (INTU) fiscal first-quarter earnings met expectations. However, the full-year revenue guidance was revised lower on Credit Karma growth. Additionally, the fintech announced a divestiture of its Mailchimp business.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended October 31, the payments technology company reported non-GAAP diluted EPS rose 56% year-over-year to $2.91 from $1.87, exceeding the S&P Global Market Intelligence's CapIQ estimate of $2.64.

Total revenue increased 12% to $4.4B, exceeding the Visible Alpha consensus of $4.31B.

Global Business Solutions revenue increased 15% to $3.1B, vs. the consensus of $3.03B. QuickBooks Online Accounting revenue increased 19% to $1.4B (in line with expectations), driven by higher effective prices, mix shift, and customer growth.

Consumer revenue increased 7% to $958M, below the $967.54M consensus. Credit Karma revenue increased 9% to $708M (vs. $719.76M consensus). TurboTax revenue increased 1% to $199M (vs. $202.55M expected). ProTax revenue increased 13% to $51M, vs. the $45.54M consensus).

Mailchimp revenue decreased 1% to $313M, vs. $310.79M expected.

Intuit has entered into a definitive agreement to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons (BSP) for ~$3.68B. The consideration consists of $3.31B in cash and $368M in Bending Spoons' stock.

The company does not expect any impact from the pending sale of Mailchimp.

"Intuit remains focused on solving businesses' biggest problems and has built AI-native experiences to help businesses win new customers, manage their pipeline, and help them grow through its lead-to-cash capabilities. Selling Mailchimp sharpens Intuit's focus behind that strategy," said the earnings release.

The transaction is expected to close in early 2027. Cash proceeds are set to be used to repurchase shares.

For the fiscal full year, the fintech lowered its revenue guidance to $23.08B-$23.37B from $23.28B-$23.51B. The metric falls short of the Visible Alpha consensus of $23.40B.

The updated revenue guidance reflects an updated consumer revenue growth guidance to 2%-4% from 4%-6%. Credit Karma growth is now estimated at 3%-7%, compared to the prior estimate of 11%-13%.

Non-GAAP EPS guidance was maintained at the range of $22.88 to $23.12, below the $28.99 Visible Alpha consensus.

The area that brings the guidance down is Credit Karma, and there the factors are twofold, CFO Sandeep Aujla told Seeking Alpha. "One is the interest rate environment is different today than when we set guidance in August. In August, we were debating whether the Fed will hold interest rates or drop interest rates."

"After the September interest rate increase, we saw consumer demand across our verticals slow down," said the CFO. "Late in the quarter, we saw our partner's pace of growth in the segments we serve slow down."

"And then, we saw the evolution in consumer behavior, particularly in how they're engaging with AI experiences, having a larger than anticipated or faster than anticipated impact on our performance. So these are factors that are impacting us here in the near term."

Credit Karma is one part of our company that is impacted by the macro cycle, said the CFO.

For the fiscal second quarter, revenue is expected to be in the range of $4.93B-$4.95B, vs. the $5.11B consensus. Non-GAAP EPS is expected to be in the range of $3.17-$3.22, vs. $3.94 CapIQ consensus.

Aujla noted that FQ2 growth will be lighter than the previous second quarters, and there are four factors driving that. One of the factors is Credit Karma. And then, the company is focused on taking a share of e-filers. They are introducing Credit Karma tax, which is a low-cost tax offering to resonate with the price-sensitive customer. 

"We expect that it'll be more of the Credit Karma tax that has an impact on the Q2 number," he said.

Then, the company sees an opportunity to bring transfer capabilities in-house instead of partnering for it. The change is expected to lead to changes in the revenue booking timeline. Furthermore, desktop revenue is expected to be "flattish" during the quarter with customers migrating to the online platform.

"I would say that these three things that are driving the Q2 guide, outside of Credit Karma, are very much in line with the strategy," he said, adding that it will be beneficial in the long-term.

The board maintained Intuit's quarterly dividend at $1.38 per share, payable on January 15.

Earnings conference call is scheduled for 1:30 PM Pacific Time today.

data.title: Wall Street ends 2% lower on Anthropic's IPO date
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages ended in the red on Thursday, as investors focused their attention on the highly anticipated public debut of artificial intelligence startup Anthropic (ANT).

The blue-chip Dow (DJI) finished -2%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) ended -1.8%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) closed -2%.

From a sector-by-sector basis, all the 11 segments concluded in negative trading territory, with consumer discretionary leading the way lower, while energy was the best-performing area.

Anthropic (ANT) made history on Thursday as it became the first pure-play AI lab with a public listing on the Nasdaq. Shares opened at $111.50, and the stock ended higher on the session by +16.8%.

"Today’s Anthropic IPO didn’t help the market, as the main issue remains unsolved. That issue is the durability of the AI buildout, as problems at Nvidia (NVDA) and even AMD (AMD) have caused investors to fear that their margins may come under pressure,” Seeking Alpha analyst Leo Nelissen of Main Street Alpha stated.

Meanwhile, for the week ended Nov. 14, initial jobless claims in the U.S. rose by 1K to 203K, edging past the 198K consensus, according to data released by the U.S. Department of Labor. 

The U.S. 2-year Treasury yield (US2Y) dipped 4 basis points to 4.76%, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) ticked lower 2 basis points to 5.04%, and the U.S. 30-year Treasury yield (US30Y) inched down 1 basis point to 5.40%. 

As for other stocks that were on the move, shares of PDD Holdings (PDD) advanced +11%, while shares of Williams-Sonoma (WSM) dropped -15%.

data.title: Rising business costs test profit growth, but investment plans hold up
data.description:
U.S. small and mid-sized businesses entered the fourth quarter with weakening profitability momentum and more cautious growth expectations, even as financing plans pointed to continued investment, according to a November 19 report from the Bank of America Institute.

The bank’s business account data showed year-over-year profitability growth was roughly flat for small firms in October and turned negative for mid-sized businesses. The figures use three-month moving averages and cover firms with annual revenue below $5 million and between $5 million and $50 million, respectively.

 

For investors, the findings suggest mounting pressure on business earnings, with meaningful differences across industries. Construction showed greater weakness, while agriculture and transportation demonstrated more resilience despite higher oil-related spending.

 

Energy costs rise

Oil-related payments per business client with less than $50 million in annual revenue rose more than 20% from a year earlier in October, measured on a three-month moving average. The category includes payments to gasoline, trucking, airline and travel-center companies, making it a spending measure rather than a direct gauge of fuel prices alone.

Construction businesses recorded declining profitability across both size groups as their oil-related payments continued to rise. By contrast, mid-sized agricultural firms posted profitability growth of nearly 6%, and transportation and warehousing businesses recorded positive growth. Oil-related payments in agriculture and transportation eased from September peaks.

Business owners’ expectations also weakened. Just 58% expected revenue to increase over the next 12 months, down from 74% in 2025, according to the bank’s annual Business Owner Report, which the Institute cited. Fewer small and mid-sized firms planned to expand, with revenue expectations deteriorating more sharply among small businesses.

Inflation remained the leading concern, cited by 75% of owners, up from 70% a year earlier. Concern about oil, gas and other commodity prices climbed to 71% from 55%, the largest increase among the issues surveyed. Concern about tariff policy declined to 60% from 64%.

The Institute suggested higher costs may increasingly be affecting margins as the benefit from tariff refunds wanes. It cautioned, however, that one month of weaker profitability momentum does not establish a broader trend.

Financing still available

Credit availability offered some support. The net share of banks reporting tighter commercial and industrial lending standards remained well below 2023 levels, according to Federal Reserve survey data cited in the report. That indicates less widespread tightening, although it does not mean borrowing has become inexpensive.

Indeed, a net 13% of small-business owners reported paying a higher interest rate on their most recent loan in October, the highest reading since August 2024, according to National Federation of Independent Business figures cited by the Institute.

Despite those pressures, 85% of business owners planned to obtain financing over the next 12 months. More than half said they had applied for a loan or credit line during the previous two years, suggesting businesses continued to see reasons to borrow.

Planned uses extended beyond covering operating costs. About half of respondents expected to spend funding on marketing and promotion, while substantial shares cited staffing, equipment and technology. For investors assessing suppliers to these businesses, those intentions suggest continued demand, although financing plans do not guarantee actual spending.

The findings require some caution: the expectations survey was conducted in August, before the October account activity analyzed in the report. It covered 849 small-business owners and 250 mid-sized business owners. The transaction data reflect selected Bank of America clients, may contain selection bias and generally are not adjusted for seasonality.

The investment question is whether businesses can sustain growth spending while absorbing higher costs. October’s results suggest that ability varies considerably by industry, making margins, pricing power and borrowing costs important measures to watch alongside revenue growth.

data.title: Plunging oil refining margins signal inflation relief for central banks
data.description:
Global oil refining margins are collapsing back toward pre-war levels, giving central banks and bond-market investors a far clearer sign of cooling inflation than falling crude (USO) (BNO) prices alone, according to Javier Blas, an energy and commodities columnist at Bloomberg.

Benchmark 3-2-1 crack spreads—which measure the theoretical profit from turning three barrels of crude into two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of diesel—have tumbled to between $25 and $40 a barrel from peaks of $60 to $75 just weeks ago, Blas noted in a social media post.

The steepest retreat has hit Asia, where Dubai-linked margins have plunged to near $20 a barrel from above $60 a barrel in October, approaching their early-2026 baseline before Middle East conflict disrupted global processing capacity. European margins tied to Brent crude (CO1:COM) have fallen over the same stretch to roughly $28 a barrel from nearly $60, while U.S. WTI (CL1:COM) margins have slipped to under $40 from highs near $70.

A sharp slide in wholesale gasoline prices has driven much of the contraction, Blas wrote, as seasonal demand slows and steady refinery output keeps fuel supplies abundant.

For monetary policymakers and fixed-income markets, narrowing refining margins carry more weight than headline crude futures because households and freight operators buy finished fuels rather than raw oil. After months in which processing bottlenecks kept pump and diesel prices elevated, the ongoing normalization in spreads removes a stubborn upside risk to consumer price growth.

data.title: UniFirst, Cintas executives to meet with FTC on Friday - CTFN
data.description:
UniFirst CEO Steven Sintros and Cintas CEO Todd Schneider are expected to have a meeting with the Federal Trade Commission on Friday.

It's not clear what will be discussed at the meeting and whether it's a “last rites” meeting, according to a CTFN report on Thursday, which cited unidentified sources. On Monday, there was a meeting between UniFirst (UNF) and Cintas (CTAS) lawyers and outside counsel  to prepare for the Friday meeting.

Semafor on Friday reported that the FTC will soon have a “last rites” meeting with the parties. These meetings between the antitrust regulator and the parties are typically a precursor to a formal lawsuit.

The latest update comes after a Semafor report late Wednesday that Cintas (CTAS) Chairman Scott Farmer met with President Donald Trump recently to try to salvage its $5.5 billion purchase of rival UniFirst (UNF), as the FTC may sue to block the combination. Farmer met with Trump to try to have him intervene, as FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson appears inclined to challenge the deal.

The president has signaled that he will defer to Ferguson's judgment, one person familiar told Semafor. A CTFN story on Friday implied that Washington, D.C. lobbyists for Cintas (CTAS) and UniFirst (UNF) may not be able to get the deal over the goal line. 

Cintas (CTAS) has engaged legal counsel and expects the FTC to file a lawsuit, according to the Semafor report. Cintas has indicated to some investors that it may seek a divestiture package to try to thwart a lawsuit, though internally the company doesn't appear to want to divest.

The UniFirst/Cintas deal spread widened to $93 on Thursday from $85 on Wednesday. The spread narrowed on Wednesday after a report indicated that the companies were cautiously optimistic that the FTC would clear the combination unconditionally and were planning for integration.

 Cintas (CTAS) agreed to acquire smaller rival UniFirst (UNF) for $310 per share in cash and stock in March, representing an enterprise value of about $5.5B.
